notes: Estate/probate case about executor's power of sale and judgment liens on a remainder interest; 'incident of ownership' language concerns real property title, not letting rooms or dwellings. No bearing on compensated occupancy.
Riparian water-rights dispute between mill and factory owners over a stream; the 'incident of ownership' selector match concerns water use rights, unrelated to lodging or letting of dwellings.
Commercial lease covenant/estoppel dispute (tenant's right to dispute landlord's title); premises are ordinary demised property, not lodging or a householder's own dwelling let short-term.

Judgment creditor's bill against a stockholder of a steamboat company for a fraudulent dividend distribution; the bailment/innkeeper selector match is from the volume's index (Bailment headnote), not the case itself. No lodging issue.
Habeas corpus proceeding to admit a convicted misdemeanant to bail pending writ of error; purely criminal procedure, no connection to letting or lodging.

Partnership dispute between hotel-keeping co-partners over which partner may take renewal leases of the hotel premises in his own name after the partnership term ends. Concerns leasehold/fiduciary law between the business partners, not the legal character of letting rooms to hotel guests or lodgers.

Marriage-brokerage contract case; plaintiff's furnishing of 'rooms, fire and light' was an incidental matchmaking service to let two people meet, not a letting of a dwelling/rooms to a lodger or boarder for occupancy. Held void as against public policy on brokerage grounds, unrelated to lodging-house doctrine.
Public-nuisance/negligence case about a cellarway extending into a sidewalk and municipal authority to permit such structures. No relation to letting rooms or lodging.
Guardian's lease of a minor's farm to a tenant-farmer and the assignability of covenants for waste/bad husbandry; agricultural leasehold dispute, not lodging or short-term dwelling letting.

holding_summary: The Court of Appeals upheld a New York City ordinance requiring owners of existing tenement houses to install water supply appliances on each occupied floor when directed by the board of health, sustaining it as a valid exercise of the police power to protect public health and reduce fire risk. The court rejected the landlord's claim that the requirement, imposed without a prior hearing or compensation for the owner's expense, violated due process. Judge Bartlett dissented, viewing the provision as an overbroad and unlimited delegation of discretion to the health department that amounted to confiscation of the landlord's control over its property.

quotes.text: We think the act is valid as an exercise of the police power with respect to the public health and also with respect to the public safety regarding fires and their extinguishment.
Laws and regulations of a police nature, though they may disturb the enjoyment of individual rights, are not unconstitutional, though no provision is made for compensation for such disturbances.

The legislature, in the exercise of this power, may direct that certain improvements shall be made in existing houses at the owners’ expense, so that the health and safety of the occupants and of the public through them may be guarded.

notes: Tenement houses here are multi-family rental buildings owned/managed by an institutional landlord (Trinity Church), not individual householders letting rooms in their own homes; treated as the adverse-side analogue since it sustains police-power regulation of multi-occupancy rental housing. Characterization left null (lease/license/lodging/innkeeping) because the case adjudicates regulatory validity, not the legal classification of the tenancy arrangement, and no quote supports any of those categories. Duration left 'unclear' as the opinion does not state length of occupancy for the tenement families.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Dispute over payment for building repairs and whether an assignment of a commercial lease as collateral security made the assignee liable as mortgagee in possession for rent. No lodging or short-term dwelling letting involved.

Widow and her minor children (co-owners of the family home) continued living rent-free in the deceased father's house; guardian later sued for use-and-occupation rent. This is an intra-family occupancy/agency dispute, not a compensated letting of rooms or a dwelling to a lodger, boarder, or stranger.

Statute of limitations tolling question turning on whether a defendant 'resided' outside New York while traveling abroad; concerns domicile/residence for limitations purposes, not letting or lodging of dwellings.
Liquor license application near a schoolhouse under the Excise Law; a schoolhouse-occupancy definitional question but no bearing on letting rooms/dwellings for lodging.
Municipal ordinances regulating railroad train speed and stopping at street crossings; a police-power case but concerning railroads, not lodging houses or letting of dwellings.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Elevated-railroad fee-damage valuation case; the fact that the lessee sublet 'furnished rooms' in the dwelling is mentioned only in passing as background to rental-value evidence. The court's holding concerns methodology for computing fee and rental damages, not the legal character of the furnished-room letting itself, so it is excluded under the 'passing mention' rule.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Defectively executed trust lease of a commercial store property (ten-year term signed by only two of three trustees), resulting in a year-to-year tenancy; ordinary commercial landlord-tenant law, unrelated to lodging.
Ejectment/deed-reformation action over land (including land under water) mistakenly included in a municipal deed description; a title/boundary dispute, not letting or lodging.
